chapter_note: The chapter opens with a brief hagiographic frame, then preserves a compact core teaching (¶2–3) describing the primordial summons and answer between the Living Spirit and the First Man as divinised “letters” containing total foreknowledge of events. From ¶4 onward the pattern is extended to the holy church, good works, and direct exhortation—consistent with the strong editorial-fatigue signal and institutional/application drift.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Formulaic hagiographic opening (“Once again he speaks to his disciples…”) functioning as a narrative container, not part of the cosmological exposition.

paragraphs.core_text: Consider the summons, which was sent from the Living Spirit in the beginning. He sent it to the First Man. It is a peace letter and greeting that he wrote and sent to his brother, in which all the tidings are written down, together with everything it will bring about and establish by that summons. That summons, the First Man [... is ordained to happen.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Impersonal, systematic cosmological teaching: primordial actors (Living Spirit / First Man) and a structural claim about foreknowledge contained in the “summons,” without institutional address or citation.

paragraphs.core_text:
⟨p.183⟩
The answer that was sent from the First Man came to the heights, to the Living Spirit. That is also a letter, which was sent from the First Man to the Living Spirit, in which all the tidings are written down; and every war and the struggles that he had waged. It did [...] in the answer that the First Man [... ...] everything that had happened and everything [that would happen], all that had been done and whatever is made ready to be done by him. The Living Spirit knew all the wars and the dangers and the contests that the rulers had waged against the First Man.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Continuation of the primordial letter-pair schema (summons/answer) entirely within the cosmic drama (wars, rulers, heights), maintaining an expository voice; slight application-score presence does not correspond to an actual audience pivot.

Editorial extension of the same “letter” motif into the institutional sphere (“sent to the holy church… as the holy church shall understand”), i.e., cosmos → contemporary church application; high Christian register supports later ecclesial redirection.
Institutional/ethical application: “good works,” fasting, prayers, entreaty, and presentation before Christ—church practice rather than cosmological mechanics.
Direct second-person exhortation (“I say to you… Everything that you will ask…”) marks application voice and pastoral instruction rather than substrate exposition.
